A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ReLU initialization and pretraining work. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite the changed title and formatting.

before.justification: v3 reports original function-approximation experiments, including dense-data training, sparse-data prediction, and comparisons of initialization and pretraining strategies in Tables 1–3.

after.justification: v4 retains those original experiments and adds non-convex and two-dimensional approximation results plus a learning-rate sensitivity study.

M1.justification: v4 turns v3's suggested assembly of component networks into an explicit extension using linear combinations and block-diagonal layers. Section 5 introduces two accumulation neurons to preserve negative components and inverted triangle functions to avoid unwanted ReLU truncation. The original one-dimensional pretraining procedure remains.

E1.justification: The four original one-dimensional targets remain. v4 additionally evaluates the non-convex function x^3 − x and the two-dimensional radial function (x^2 + y^2)^(3/2), substantially extending the represented function classes and input dimensionality.

E2.justification: Tables 1–3 retain the same comparator membership, including Default Network, RAAI, and the pretraining variants where originally evaluated. The new examples reuse standard initialization as the comparator. KAN and other newly discussed methods are not experimentally benchmarked.

E3.justification: Section 4.1 changes the reported Adam learning rate from 0.0001 to 0.001 while retaining the original network dimensions, data sampling, and training budgets. Added studies introduce 8 × 5 comparison networks and a learning-rate sweep. Identical original table values do not establish whether those experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Appendix A.7 adds a sensitivity analysis varying the learning rate for x^3 under a fixed 1,000-epoch budget. Section 5 also examines structural breakdown in the combined network. The original pretraining and differentiability ablations and neuron-level analyses remain.

E5.justification: The original minimum/mean reporting over 30 models is unchanged. Figure 12 uses the existing best-of-30 reporting practice rather than introducing a new uncertainty procedure. Neither version reports confidence intervals, significance tests, or dispersion estimates.

E6.justification: All 48 numerical entries in Tables 1–3 are unchanged. New Figures 7–8 report losses of 4 × 10^-7 versus 8 × 10^-6 for x^3 − x, and 3.5 × 10^-6 versus 1.5 × 10^-4 for the radial task, comparing combined components with standard networks. Figure 12 adds learning-rate-dependent results. These are new comparisons, not cross-version performance gains.

T1.justification: Lemma 7.9 becomes Lemma A.9 and changes its conclusion from convexity to concavity, consistent with the decreasing-derivative argument. Its limit proof also corrects the interior-point comparison from f_i(c) to f_i(b). Section 3 excludes triangle-peak endpoints explicitly. The main scaling theorem and most appendix derivations are retained.

C1.justification: v3's abstract and conclusion restrict demonstrated benefits to convex, one-dimensional functions and leave broader applicability to future work. v4 explicitly claims demonstrated benefits for non-convex and multidimensional functions, expanding the scope of the paper's principal contribution.

C2.justification: v4 reframes the single-component expressivity limitations around combining components and attributes subsequent structural breakdown to training initially zero off-block weights. It adds an initialization-bias explanation for very small learning rates and softens Section 4.2's claim about eliminating problematic local minima. The second-derivative restriction remains in Appendix A.5.

D1.justification: For the new extension, Section 5 documents block-diagonal implementation and sign handling, while Figure 9 specifies omitting ReLU between component blocks. The original weight matrices, pseudocode, and disclosure of 1,000 epochs per training phase were already present in v3.

R1.justification: v4 substantially expands positioning through its comparison with KAN and discussion of difference-of-convex representations. It acknowledges prior nonsymmetric triangle/folding constructions and contrasts reparameterization with Park et al.'s loss-based approach to increasing linear regions. The original approximation and initialization literature remains.

P1.justification: v4 retitles the paper, replaces much of the 'compositional network' terminology with initialization/pretraining language, and rewrites substantial related-work and method exposition. The limitations-led Section 5 becomes an extension-led narrative, accompanied by a substantially revised conclusion.

P2.justification: v4 adds Figures 7–9 and 12, covering extension results, network assembly, and learning-rate sensitivity. Original appendix Figures 7–8 survive as Figures 10–11. A document-wide template change revises the title block, headers, heading typography, and figure placement; the original table structures remain.

improvement.justification: v4 provides a concrete extension with two demonstrations, tests learning-rate sensitivity, and corrects a convexity/concavity error and its associated proof step. These improve empirical support and mathematical clarity. The net gain remains limited by sparse protocol detail for the new examples and the unexplained learning-rate revision alongside identical original tables.
